Returns the position of the [`Hitbox`] in the frame's front-to-back order.

Zero is the frontmost hitbox. Larger values are farther from the viewer.
doc_texts.fn:HitTestEntry::tags: Returns the tags that were attached to the [`Hitbox`] when it was inserted.
doc_texts.fn:Hitbox::contains:
Returns whether `point` lies inside this hitbox's content mask and its bounds.

This check ignores occlusion, so a point can be inside a hitbox that is
covered by another one. Use [`Hitbox::is_hovered`] to check what the
mouse is actually over.
doc_texts.fn:Hitbox::is_hovered:
Returns whether the mouse is over this hitbox, for hover styles and mouse handlers.

This returns `false` when a hitbox in front of this one blocks the mouse,
with [`InteractiveElement::occlude`](crate::InteractiveElement::occlude) or [`InteractiveElement::block_mouse_except_scroll`](crate::InteractiveElement::block_mouse_except_scroll).
It also returns `false` during keyboard input, so keyboard navigation doesn't
show hover styles. Use this for clicks, moves and hover styling. For scroll
handling, use [`Hitbox::should_handle_scroll`], because a scrollable container
under an overlay should still scroll.
doc_texts.fn:Hitbox::is_hovered_at:
Checks whether this hitbox would be hovered at `position`, regardless of the current input
modality or mouse position.
doc_texts.fn:Hitbox::should_handle_scroll:
Returns whether the mouse is over this hitbox and this hitbox should handle scroll events.

Use it in `ScrollWheelEvent` handlers. It returns `false` only when a
[`HitboxBehavior::BlockMouse`] hitbox is in front of this one, so overlays
can block clicks without blocking scrolling underneath.
doc_texts.fn:HitboxBehavior::blocks_mouse: Returns `true` if hitboxes behind this one can't be hovered.
doc_texts.fn:HitboxBehavior::occludes: Returns `true` if hitboxes behind this one can't be hovered or scrolled.
doc_texts.fn:HitboxId::is_hovered:
Returns whether the mouse is over this hitbox and it isn't covered by a blocking hitbox.

Always `true` if this hitbox has captured the pointer. Returns `false`
during keyboard input, so keyboard navigation hides hover styles. See
[`Hitbox::is_hovered`] for details.
doc_texts.fn:HitboxId::placeholder:
Returns an id that is valid for tests which need a [`HitboxId`] but don't use its value.

Only available with the `test-support` feature. Don't pass it to window methods
that look up a real hitbox.
doc_texts.fn:HitboxId::should_handle_scroll:
Returns whether the mouse is over this hitbox and it should handle scroll events.

Use this for `ScrollWheelEvent` handlers, and [`HitboxId::is_hovered`] for
everything else. See [`Hitbox::is_hovered`] for why the two differ.
doc_texts.fn:Image::bytes: Returns the encoded image bytes.
doc_texts.fn:Image::empty: Returns a PNG image with no bytes. It can't be decoded.
doc_texts.fn:Image::format: Returns the image's format.
doc_texts.fn:Image::from_bytes:
Creates an image from `format` and encoded `bytes`.

The [`Image::id`] is a hash of `bytes` alone, so two images with the same bytes but different formats share an id.
doc_texts.fn:Image::get_render_image: Returns the decoded image if it's already cached. Doesn't start a load.
doc_texts.fn:Image::id: Returns the image's cache key. [`Image::from_bytes`] sets it from a hash of the bytes.
doc_texts.fn:Image::is_asset_cached:
Check whether this image is present in GPUI's asset cache (loading or
loaded), without fetching it.
doc_texts.fn:Image::remove_asset: Removes the decoded image from GPUI's asset cache.
doc_texts.fn:Image::to_image_data:
Decodes the image into a [`RenderImage`] that you can paint.

SVG images are rendered at scale `1.0`.

# Errors

Returns an error if the bytes can't be decoded. For a GIF, frames that fail to
decode are skipped and logged, and an error is returned only when every frame fails.
doc_texts.fn:Image::use_render_image:
Returns the decoded image, starting the load if it isn't cached yet.

Returns `None` while the image is loading, or if it can't be decoded. Call it from a render method, so the window redraws when the load finishes.
doc_texts.fn:ImageCacheItem::get: Returns the cached result without subscribing to completion notifications.
doc_texts.fn:ImageCacheItem::new: Starts loading an image into a new cache entry.
doc_texts.fn:ImageCacheItem::use_image: Returns the cached result or subscribes the current view to completion.
doc_texts.fn:ImageFormat::extension: Returns the file extension for this image format (without leading dot).
doc_texts.fn:ImageFormat::mime_type: Returns the canonical MIME type, such as `image/png`.
doc_texts.fn:ImageSource::is_asset_cached:
Returns `true` if this source is loading or loaded in the app's asset cache. Starts no load.

Available with the `test-support` feature. Use it in tests to check that an image was
requested or evicted.
doc_texts.fn:ImageSource::remove_asset:
Evicts this source from the app's asset cache, so the next `img` that uses it loads it again.

Only [`ImageSource::Resource`] and [`ImageSource::Image`] are in that cache, so the other
variants do nothing. Images held by an [`crate::image_cache`] element are not affected.
doc_texts.fn:Img::image_cache:
Uses `image_cache` for this image, instead of the cache from an ancestor.

Without this call, the image uses the cache of the nearest ancestor [`crate::image_cache`] element,
or the app-wide asset cache if there is none. Only [`ImageSource::Resource`] sources go
through an image cache. The other variants ignore it.
doc_texts.fn:InlineLayout::paint:
Paints the glyphs and underlines or strikethroughs of the inline layout.

`origin` is the top-left corner of the layout's box. This method paints
only text. The atomic boxes in [`InlineLayout::boxes`] are not painted here.
doc_texts.fn:InlineLayout::paint_background:
Paints the background color of each text run in the inline layout.

`origin` is the top-left corner of the layout's box. Call this before
[`InlineLayout::paint`].
doc_texts.fn:Inspector::active_element_id:
Returns the ID of the element that is hovered while picking, or the element
that was selected, or `None` if no element is active.
doc_texts.fn:Inspector::is_picking: Returns `true` while the inspector is in picking mode.
doc_texts.fn:Inspector::render_inspector_states:
Returns one element for each state type held by the active element when that type has
a renderer registered with [`App::register_inspector_element`]. Returns an empty list
when no element is active.

Call this from your inspector renderer to show per-element details.
doc_texts.fn:Inspector::start_picking:
Enters picking mode. While picking, moving the pointer over an element makes it
the active element, and a click selects it and leaves picking mode.
doc_texts.fn:InteractiveText::new:
Creates an interactive text element with the given ID and styled text.

The ID must be unique among siblings. It keys the mouse state that
survives between frames.
doc_texts.fn:InteractiveText::on_click:
Calls `listener` when the user presses and releases the mouse inside one of `ranges`.

The listener receives the index in `ranges` of the matching range. The press
and the release must both fall inside the same range. A press in one range
and a release in another calls nothing. If the ranges overlap, the listener
runs once for each range that contains both points.
doc_texts.fn:InteractiveText::on_hover:
Calls `listener` as the mouse moves over the text.

The listener receives the byte index of the character under the mouse, or
`None` when the mouse is over the element but not over a character. It runs only
when that value changes, and not when the mouse leaves the element. It also
receives the [`MouseMoveEvent`].
doc_texts.fn:InteractiveText::tooltip:
Sets a tooltip for each character, as chosen by `builder`.

`builder` receives the byte index of the character under the mouse. It returns
the view to show as the tooltip, or `None` for no tooltip at that character.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::block_mouse_except_scr:
Stops mouse interactions from reaching elements behind this element, but lets scroll events through.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::block_mouse_except_scroll`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::can_drop:
Sets a predicate that decides whether this element accepts the value being dragged.

The predicate runs only while the pointer is over the element, and it receives the dragged value.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::can_drop`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_action:
Runs `listener` when an action of type `A` is dispatched to this element, during the capture phase.

The capture phase runs before the bubble phase. If the listener does not call [`App::stop_propagation`],
dispatch continues to the bubble handlers. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::capture_action`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_any_mouse_down:
Runs `listener` for a press of any button over this element, during the capture phase.

Use it to see a press before the element on top handles it. The listener runs only while the pointer is over
the element. This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::capture_any_mouse_down`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_any_mouse_up:
Runs `listener` for a release of any button over this element, during the capture phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::capture_any_mouse_up`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_key_down:
Runs `listener` for key presses during the capture phase. Like [`on_key_down`](Self::on_key_down), it runs only
if no action bound to the keystroke handled it.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::capture_key_down`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_key_up:
Runs `listener` for key releases during the capture phase.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::capture_key_up`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_mouse_pressure:
Runs `listener` for pressure changes over this element, during the capture phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::capture_mouse_pressure`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::capture_pinch:
Runs `listener` for pinch gestures during the capture phase, whether or not the pointer is over the element.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::capture_pinch`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::compute_style:
Computes the visual style of this element for its current state.

The result includes the base style, plus any focus, hover, active and drag-over styles that apply at the moment.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::cursor_with:
Resolves this element's cursor from pointer position and bounds.
Return `None` to defer to another cursor request.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::external_drag_payload:
Registers a resolver for the data to offer the platform when a drag from this element leaves the window.

The resolver runs at most once for each drag, when the pointer leaves the window. It must be called after
[`Interactivity::on_drag`] and with the same dragged type `T`. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`StatefulInteractiveElement::external_drag_payload`].

# Panics

Panics in debug builds if called before [`Interactivity::on_drag_alt`] or [`Interactivity::on_drag`]. If called
twice on the same element, it panics in debug builds when a drag starts.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::hover_listener_mode:
Sets how [`Self::on_hover`] responds to key presses while the mouse is stationary.
This affects only the hover listener, not hover styles or tooltips. The imperative API
equivalent to [`StatefulInteractiveElement::hover_listener_mode`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::hoverable_tooltip:
Sets a function that builds a tooltip view that stays open while the pointer is over it.

This is the same as [`Interactivity::tooltip`], except the pointer can move into the tooltip without closing it.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::hoverable_tooltip`].

# Panics

Panics in debug builds if a tooltip is already set on this element.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::occlude_mouse:
Stops the mouse from reaching elements behind this element.

Use [`Interactivity::block_mouse_except_scroll`] for most cases, because it still lets scroll events reach
the elements behind. This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::occlude`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_any_mouse_down:
Runs `listener` for a press of any button over this element, during the bubble phase.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_any_mouse_down`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_any_mouse_up:
Runs `listener` for a release of any button over this element, during the bubble phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_aux_click:
Runs `listener` for clicks with a button other than the left one.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_aux_click`]. It requires an element id.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_boxed_action:
Runs `listener` when an action of the same type as `action` is dispatched, during the bubble phase.

Use this when the action type is only known at runtime, such as when a component accepts actions from its
caller. The listener receives the `action` value passed here, not the dispatched action, so only its type is
used for matching. This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_boxed_action`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_click:
Runs `listener` when this element is clicked, or when it is activated from the keyboard.

A mouse click fires when the left button is pressed and released over the element without the pointer
moving far enough to start a drag. A keyboard click fires when Enter or Space is pressed and released while
the element is focused and no other key is pressed in between. The listener receives a [`ClickEvent`].
This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_click`]. It requires an element id.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drag:
Starts a drag of `value` when the left button is pressed on this element and the pointer moves.

The `constructor` runs when the drag starts. It receives the value and the cursor offset from the element's
origin, and returns the view that is drawn under the pointer. Any dragged value must be `'static`.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_drag`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drag_alt:
Sets the function that starts a drag from this element.

The function receives the cursor offset and the cursor style, and returns an [`AnyDrag`]. Use
[`Interactivity::on_drag`] unless you need to build the [`AnyDrag`] yourself.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_drag_alt`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drag_move:
Runs `listener` for pointer moves during a drag of type `T`, in the capture phase.

The listener runs for every move while a drag of type `T` is active, including moves outside this element.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_drag_move`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drag_over_any:
Sets a style function that applies while a dragged value is over this element.

The style applies only if this element has a drop listener for the dragged type. Use
[`DropListener::on_drag_over`] when the style depends on the dragged type. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_drag_over_any`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drop:
Runs `listener` when a drag of type `T` is released over this element.

The drop runs whether or not the drag started on this element. Use [`InteractiveElement::can_drop`] or a
[`DropListener`] to refuse drops. This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_drop`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_drop_alt:
Attaches a [`DropListener`] that handles drags of type `T` over this element.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_drop_alt`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_file_drop_exit:
Bind the given callback to [`FileDropEvent::Exited`] when a platform file drag
leaves this element's window while the element is hovered.

This is a window-local exit event, not notification that the platform drag session ended.
The imperative API equivalent to [`InteractiveElement::on_file_drop_exit`].

See [`Context::listener`](crate::Context::listener) to get access to a view's state from this callback.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_hover:
Runs `listener` with `true` when the pointer enters this element and with `false` when it leaves.

Transitions caused by layout changes under a stationary pointer also run the listener. The listener does not
run while a drag is in progress. This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_hover`].

After keyboard input, hover stays off until the pointer moves, a button is pressed or the screen is touched. Set
[`HoverListenerMode::InputModalityIndependent`] with [`Self::hover_listener_mode`] to keep tracking it.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_hover_region:
Calls `listener` when the projected pointer value changes.
The projection receives window coordinates and element bounds; return `None` outside active regions.
Layout changes and occlusion are observed independently of event propagation.
Keep listener order stable across renders.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_key_down:
Runs `listener` for key presses, during the bubble phase.

The listener runs only if no action bound to the keystroke handled it. The element must be on the focus path.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_key_down`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_key_up:
Runs `listener` for key releases, during the bubble phase.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_key_up`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_modifiers_changed:
Runs `listener` when the set of pressed modifier keys changes.

The event is delivered along the focus path, from the focused element upward. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_modifiers_changed`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_down:
Runs `listener` when `button` is pressed over this element.

The listener runs in the bubble phase, and only if the pointer is over the element's hitbox.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_down`]. Prefer the fluent method
when you are building an element in a single chain.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_down_all:
Runs `listener` for every mouse press, in both phases, whether or not the pointer is over the element.

The listener receives the phase, the element's hitbox, and the event. Check the phase yourself.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_down_all`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_down_out:
Runs `listener` for a press of any button outside this element, during the capture phase.

The listener does not run while a window prompt is open. Use it to close a popover when the user clicks elsewhere.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_down_out`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_exit:
Runs `listener` when the pointer leaves the window while it is over this element.

This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_exit`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_move:
Runs `listener` when the pointer moves over this element, during the bubble phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element's hitbox. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_move`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_move_all:
Runs `listener` for every mouse move, whether or not the pointer is over the element.

The listener receives the phase, the element's hitbox, and the event. Use it to track the pointer while a
drag is in progress outside the element. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_move_all`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_pressure:
Runs `listener` for pressure changes over this element, during the bubble phase.

Pressure events come from force-sensitive trackpads, which report them only on macOS today. The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_pressure`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_up:
Runs `listener` when `button` is released over this element, during the bubble phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_up`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_up_all:
Runs `listener` for every mouse release, in both phases, whether or not the pointer is over the element.

The listener receives the phase, the element's hitbox, and the event. Check the phase yourself.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_up_all`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_mouse_up_out:
Runs `listener` when `button` is released outside this element, during the capture phase.

The listener runs only if the pointer is not over the element's hitbox at the time of the release.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_mouse_up_out`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_pinch:
Runs `listener` for pinch gestures over this element, during the bubble phase.

The listener runs only while the pointer is over the element's hitbox. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`InteractiveElement::on_pinch`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_prepaint:
Runs `listener` during prepaint, once the element's bounds and content size are known.

The listener is consumed each frame, so register it again on every render. This is the imperative equivalent of
[`StatefulInteractiveElement::on_prepaint`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::on_scroll_wheel:
Runs `listener` for scroll wheel events at the pointer, during the bubble phase.

The innermost element runs first. The event continues to ancestors unless a listener calls
[`App::stop_propagation`], and elements behind an [`occlude`](InteractiveElement::occlude) hitbox don't receive it.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::on_scroll_wheel`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::paint:
Paints this element's background, borders and shadows, and registers its listeners with the window.

`f` runs the painting of the element's contents, and receives the final style. Call it from an element's
`paint` method, with the hitbox returned from prepaint.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::prepaint:
Commits the bounds of this element, computes its final style and hitbox, and then runs `f`.

`f` receives the computed style, the scroll offset, and the element's hitbox if one was inserted. Prepaint listeners
registered with [`Interactivity::on_prepaint`] run before `f`.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::request_layout:
Lays out this element using its configured styles.

`f` receives the computed [`Style`] and returns the [`LayoutId`] for the element. Call it from an element's
`request_layout` to apply the element's listeners, styles and state to its layout.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::set_scroll_offset:
Sets the scroll offset of the element, for use during layout.

Does nothing unless the element's style has `overflow` set to scroll on an axis. Call it from
`request_layout`, before the children are laid out.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::source_location:
Returns where this `Interactivity` was created, if the caller location was recorded.

The location is recorded in debug builds and with the `inspector` feature, and is `None` otherwise.
The inspector uses it to point at the code that created an element.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::tooltip:
Sets a function that builds a tooltip view shown while the pointer rests over this element.

The tooltip is hidden as soon as the pointer leaves the element, so the user cannot move onto it. Use
[`Interactivity::hoverable_tooltip`] for a tooltip that stays open. A long press on a touch screen also shows
it. This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::tooltip`].

# Panics

Panics in debug builds if a tooltip is already set on this element.
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::tooltip_show_delay:
Sets how long the pointer must rest over this element before its tooltip appears.

The default is 500 milliseconds. A long press on a touch screen shows the tooltip as soon as it's recognized.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::tooltip_show_delay`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::window_control_area:
Marks this element's bounds as a window control area, such as a title bar button.

The platform uses `area` to decide what clicks and drags here do, such as moving or closing the window.
This is the imperative equivalent of [`InteractiveElement::window_control_area`].
doc_texts.fn:Interactivity::write_a11y_info:
Writes this element's accessibility metadata and actions to an AccessKit node.

A custom element that composes an `Interactivity` calls this from its
[`Element::write_a11y_info`] so the fluent accessibility properties land on its own node.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::action: Returns the action this binding runs.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::action_input: Returns the JSON input the action was built from, if the binding came from a keymap file.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::keystrokes:
Returns the keystrokes that trigger this binding, in order. A binding has one keystroke
for a single key, and more for a sequence such as `ctrl-k ctrl-s`.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::load:
Creates a binding from the parts that a keymap file provides.

`keystrokes` is split on spaces and each part is parsed with [`Keystroke::parse`]. Each
keystroke is then passed to `keyboard_mapper`, and `use_key_equivalents` asks it for the
layout-dependent mapping. On macOS, that replaces a key with the character the current
layout types for it. For bindings from a keymap file, `action_input` is the JSON the action
was built from. Pass `None` when there is none.

# Errors

Returns [`InvalidKeystrokeError`] if any keystroke fails to parse. The context is already
parsed, so this function doesn't check it.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::meta: Returns the source metadata set with [`KeyBinding::with_meta`], if any.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::new:
Creates a binding that runs `action` when `keystrokes` is typed in `context`.

`keystrokes` is a whitespace-separated sequence of
[keystrokes](Keystroke::parse), such as `"cmd-s"` or `"ctrl-k ctrl-s"`.
`context` is a [key context predicate](KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse),
such as `"Editor"` or `"Editor && mode == insert"`. Pass `None` to make the binding apply
everywhere, which counts as the deepest context for precedence.

Bindings made here use the keys as written. They never go through the platform's keyboard
mapping, so use this for bindings in code.

# Panics

Panics if any keystroke or the context fails to parse. Use [`KeyBinding::load`] to get an
error instead.

# Examples

```standalone_crate
use gpui::{KeyBinding, actions};

actions!(binding_new_docs, [Save]);

let binding = KeyBinding::new("secondary-s", Save, Some("Editor"));
assert_eq!(binding.keystrokes().len(), 1);
```
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::predicate:
Returns the key context predicate this binding applies in, or `None` if it applies in
every context.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::set_meta: Sets the source metadata for this binding. See [`KeyBinding::with_meta`].
doc_texts.fn:KeyBinding::with_meta:
Sets the source metadata for this binding and returns it.

See [`KeyBindingMetaIndex`] for how the keymap uses this. A binding without metadata
counts as the strongest source.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBindingContextPredicate::eval:
Returns whether the predicate matches the whole of `contexts`, which is ordered from the
root to the focused element.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBindingContextPredicate::eval_inne:
Returns whether the predicate matches the prefix `contexts`, ordered from the root to the
focused element. `all_contexts` is the full stack, which `!` checks against.

Callers that want the whole stack use [`eval`](Self::eval). [`depth_of`](Self::depth_of)
calls this with each prefix.
doc_texts.fn:KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse:
Parses a predicate such as `Editor && !ReadOnly` or `Panel > Editor`.

The grammar, from the tightest-binding rule to the loosest, is:

- **Atoms.** An identifier, such as `Editor`, matches a context with that name. An identifier
  is letters, digits, `_` and `-`. The characters `>`, `<`, `~`, `"` and `?` can also
  appear after the first character, so write `Panel > Editor` with spaces. The text
  `Panel>Editor` is one identifier.
- **Parentheses.** `( ... )` groups a predicate.
- **Negation.** `!` applies to the atom or parenthesized group after it, so `!a && b` is
  `(!a) && b`. Use `!(a && b)` to negate a group.
- **Equality.** `key == value` and `key != value` compare the value of an entry. Both sides
  must be plain identifiers, so `mode == "full"` is an error.
- **`&&`** binds tighter than **`||`**. So `a || b && c` is `a || (b && c)`.
- **Descendant.** `parent > child` binds loosest, so `a && b > c` is `(a && b) > c`. It is
  left-associative: `A > B > C` is `(A > B) > C`.

The keymap guide has the same rules as a table.

# Errors

Returns an error for an unbalanced parenthesis, a missing operand, an operator the grammar
doesn't have, a `==` or `!=` whose operands aren't identifiers, or any leftover text.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::KeyBindingContextPredicate;
let predicate = KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse("Pane > (Editor || Terminal) && !ReadOnly")
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(predicate.to_string(), "Pane > (Editor || Terminal) && !ReadOnly");
assert!(KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse("mode == \"full\"").is_err());
```

See [contexts](crate::_documentation::concepts::contexts) and
[keyboard input](crate::_documentation::guides::keyboard) for when contexts apply.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::add: Adds an identifier, unless this context already has an entry with that key.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::contains: Returns whether this context has an entry with `key`, whether or not that entry has a value.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::extend: Adds each entry of `other` whose key this context doesn't already have.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::get:
Returns the value of the first entry with `key`. Returns `None` if there is no such entry,
or if the entry is a plain identifier.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::is_empty: Returns whether this context has no entries.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::new_with_defaults:
Creates an empty context that already has an `os` entry for the current platform.

The value is `macos`, `linux`, `windows` or `unknown`, so a binding can use
`os == macos` to apply on one platform only.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::parse:
Parses a context such as `Editor` or `Editor mode=full`.

The text is a list of entries separated by whitespace. Each entry is either an identifier,
such as `Editor`, or a key-value pair written `key=value` or `key = value`. Identifier
characters are letters, digits, `_` and `-`. An entry whose key is already present is
ignored, so the first one wins. Returns an error for text that isn't a list of such
entries, such as `.` or `=insert`.

This takes entries only. Operators such as `&&` and `>` aren't part of this format. Use
[`KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse`] to write a predicate.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::{KeyContext, SharedString};
let context = KeyContext::parse("Panel Editor mode = insert").unwrap();
assert!(context.contains("Panel"));
assert_eq!(context.primary().unwrap().key, SharedString::from("Panel"));
```
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::primary:
Returns the first identifier without a value, which names the element in
the usual context convention. Returns `None` if there is no identifier.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::secondary: Returns every entry except the one [`primary`](Self::primary) returns.
doc_texts.fn:KeyContext::set: Adds a key-value pair, unless this context already has an entry with that key.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::from_keystroke: Creates a keybinding keystroke from `keystroke` with no platform-specific mapping.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::inner: Returns the [`Keystroke`] that matching uses.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::key:
Returns the key.

Platform-specific behavior:
- On macOS and Linux, this key is the same as `inner.key`, which is the GPUI representation of the keystroke.
- On Windows, this key is the display key, for example, a `ctrl-@` keystroke will have `inner.key` as `@` and `display_key` as `2`.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::modifiers:
Returns the modifiers.

Platform-specific behavior:
- On macOS and Linux, this modifiers is the same as `inner.modifiers`, which is the GPUI representation of the keystroke.
- On Windows, this modifiers is the display modifiers, for example, a `ctrl-@` keystroke will have `inner.modifiers` as
`Modifiers::control()` and `display_modifiers` as `Modifiers::control_shift()`.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::new_with_mapper:
Creates a keybinding keystroke from `inner`, mapped by `keyboard_mapper`.

The platform's [`PlatformKeyboardMapper`](crate::PlatformKeyboardMapper) decides what
changes. On macOS, when `use_key_equivalents` is true and the current layout types a
different character for the key, the key is replaced with that character.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::remove_key_char: Clears `key_char`, so that matching and display use only `key` and the modifiers.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::set_key: Sets the key. On Windows this modifies both `inner.key` and `display_key`.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::set_modifiers: Sets the modifiers. On Windows this modifies both `inner.modifiers` and `display_modifiers`.
doc_texts.fn:KeybindingKeystroke::unparse:
Returns text that [`Keystroke::parse`] reads back as this keystroke, using the displayed
modifiers and key on Windows. See [`Keystroke::unparse`].
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::add_bindings:
Adds `bindings` after the existing ones and changes the [`version`](Self::version).

A binding added later wins over an earlier one at the same depth. Add the user's bindings
after the defaults so that they take precedence.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::all_bindings_for_input:
Returns every binding that matches all of `input`, ignoring key contexts.

The bindings are in precedence order: the most recently added comes first. Bindings that
need more keystrokes than `input` are left out. `NoAction` and `Unbind` entries that match
are included, but their effect on other bindings is not applied.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::bindings:
Iterates over all bindings, in the order they were added.

The iterator includes [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) and [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) entries.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::bindings_for_action:
Iterates over the bindings that run `action`, in the order they were added.

Bindings disabled by a later [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) or [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) are
left out. This ignores key contexts, so a binding is included even when it can't fire in the
current focus. To find the bindings that apply now, use
[`Window::bindings_for_action`](crate::Window::bindings_for_action). For a shortcut label,
use the last binding, which was added most recently.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::bindings_for_input:
Returns the bindings that match `input` in `context_stack`, and whether a longer input
could still match a binding.

The first value holds the matching bindings, highest precedence first. The second value is
`true` when some binding needs more keystrokes than `input`, so the caller should wait for
the next keystroke.

Precedence works as follows:

- **Depth.** A binding's depth is the deepest point in `context_stack` where its predicate
  matches. A binding in a deeper context wins over one in a shallower context. A binding
  without a context is as deep as the stack, so it is at least as deep as any
  context-specific binding. At equal depth, the order rule below decides.
- **Order.** At the same depth, the binding added later wins.
- **`NoAction`.** A winning [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) removes the lower-precedence
  bindings for the same keystrokes, unless they come from a stronger source. See
  [`KeyBindingMetaIndex`](crate::KeyBindingMetaIndex).
- **`Unbind`.** A winning [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) removes the lower-precedence binding for
  the same keystrokes that runs the action it names, whatever that binding's context.

Several bindings can be returned, because a match that isn't suppressed stays in the list.

# Examples

```standalone_crate
use gpui::{Action, KeyBinding, KeyContext, Keymap, Keystroke, actions};

actions!(input_docs, [Save, Format]);

let keymap = Keymap::new(vec![
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Format, Some("Workspace")),
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Save, Some("Editor")),
]);

// The `Editor` binding is at depth 2 and the `Workspace` binding at depth 1.
let (bindings, _) = keymap.bindings_for_input(
    &[Keystroke::parse("cmd-s").unwrap()],
    &[
        KeyContext::parse("Workspace").unwrap(),
        KeyContext::parse("Editor").unwrap(),
    ],
);
assert_eq!(bindings[0].action().name(), "input_docs::Save");
```
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::clear: Removes every binding and changes the [`version`](Self::version).
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::new: Creates a keymap that contains `bindings`, in the order given.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::possible_next_bindings_for_in:
Returns the bindings that `input` could still complete with more keystrokes, highest
precedence first, for the given `context_stack`.

Use it to list the shortcuts available after a prefix, such as after `ctrl-k`. Bindings
that match `input` exactly, and `NoAction` and `Unbind` entries, are not included.
doc_texts.fn:Keymap::version: Returns the current version. See [`KeymapVersion`].
doc_texts.fn:Keystroke::is_ime_in_progress:
Returns whether an input method is still composing text for this keystroke.

This is true when `key_char` is `None`, the key is printable or empty (not a named key such
as `escape` or `f1`), and none of `cmd`, `ctrl`, `fn` or `alt` is held. `shift` alone
doesn't count.
doc_texts.fn:Keystroke::parse:
Parses a keystroke from text such as `cmd-s`, `ctrl-shift-tab` or `cmd--`.

The syntax is zero or more modifiers, then a key, separated by `-`:

- **Modifiers** are `ctrl`, `alt`, `shift`, `fn`, `secondary`, `cmd`, `super` and `win`.
  They can come in any order and any case. `cmd`, `super` and `win` all set
  [`Modifiers::platform`]. `secondary` sets `cmd` on macOS and `ctrl` on other platforms,
  which is what [`Modifiers::secondary`] reports.
- **The key** is the last part. Any other part must be a modifier. Key names are
  case-insensitive and stored in lowercase, so `Tab` and `tab` are the same key. Other
  text is accepted as a key without checking, but the names that platforms produce are
  `space`, `tab`, `enter`, `backspace`, `escape`, `delete`, `insert`, `home`, `end`,
  `pageup`, `pagedown`, `up`, `down`, `left`, `right` and function keys such as `f1`.
- **A single uppercase letter** sets `shift` and uses the lowercase letter as the key, so
  `S` is `shift-s`.
- **A key of `-`** is written as an extra dash, so `cmd--` is `cmd` and `-`.
- **A modifier with no key** becomes the key. The first of `shift`, `ctrl`, `alt`, `cmd` and
  `fn` that is present is used, in that order. Its key is named `shift`, `control`, `alt`,
  `platform` or `function`, and that modifier is cleared. So `ctrl` alone is the key
  `control` with no modifiers set.
- **`key->key_char`** sets `key_char` to the text after `->`, for example `alt-s->ß`.
  [`Keystroke::should_match`] ignores it when matching a binding.

# Errors

Returns [`InvalidKeystrokeError`] if a part before the key isn't a modifier, as in
`ctrl-a-b`, or if `->` isn't followed by a key character.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::Keystroke;
let save = Keystroke::parse("secondary-s").unwrap();
assert!(save.modifiers.secondary());
assert_eq!(save.key, "s");

let shifted = Keystroke::parse("S").unwrap();
assert!(shifted.modifiers.shift);
assert_eq!(shifted.key, "s");

assert!(Keystroke::parse("ctrl-a-b").is_err());
```

See [keyboard input](crate::_documentation::guides::keyboard) for how bindings use these.
doc_texts.fn:Keystroke::should_match:
Returns whether this keystroke, as typed, matches a keystroke in a keymap.

`self` is the keystroke the user typed and `target` is the one from the binding. Matching
first compares modifiers and key. It also accepts a `target` whose key is this keystroke's
`key_char`, when the target's modifiers are exactly this keystroke's `ctrl` and `cmd` (on
Windows, when the target has no modifiers). That covers layouts where a binding
key sits behind option, such as `$` on a Czech keyboard typed as `alt-ç`, and input methods
that turn a sequence of keys into one character.
doc_texts.fn:Keystroke::unparse:
Returns text that [`Keystroke::parse`] reads back as this keystroke.

The platform's name for `cmd` is used: `cmd` on macOS, `super` on Linux and `win` on
Windows. `key_char` is not included, so the result doesn't round-trip when it is set.
doc_texts.fn:Keystroke::with_simulated_ime:
Returns this keystroke with `key_char` set to the text it would type.

Simulated keystrokes use this so that they type text as a real key press does. It only
applies when `key_char` is `None` and none of `cmd`, `ctrl`, `fn` or `alt` is held. `space`,
`tab` and `enter` type a space, a tab and a newline. Other printable keys type their
character, uppercased when `shift` is held.
doc_texts.fn:LinearColorStop::opacity:
Returns a copy of this stop with its alpha multiplied by `factor`.

The factor is clamped to `0.0..=1.0`, as with [`ColorExt::opacity`].
doc_texts.fn:List::with_sizing_behavior:
Sets whether the list sizes itself from its style or from its rows.

[`ListSizingBehavior::Auto`], the default, takes the size from the style. With
[`ListSizingBehavior::Infer`], the list is as tall as its rows, up to the space its parent gives it.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::bounds_for_item:
Returns the bounds of row `ix` in window coordinates, or `None` if the row is above the scroll
position or has not been measured.

A measured row below the viewport still has bounds, so compare them with
[`Self::viewport_bounds`]. [`Self::item_is_above_viewport`] and
[`Self::item_is_below_viewport`] answer that directly.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::is_following_tail:
Returns whether the list is following the tail right now.

This is true after [`Self::set_follow_mode`] with [`FollowMode::Tail`], until the user scrolls
toward the start or [`Self::pause_following_tail`] is called. It is false in
[`FollowMode::Normal`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::is_scrollbar_dragging:
Returns whether the scrollbar is being dragged.

This is true between [`Self::scrollbar_drag_started`] and [`Self::scrollbar_drag_ended`].
Use it to tell a scrollbar drag from a wheel or trackpad scroll, for example to stop
auto-scrolling during a manual drag.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::item_is_above_viewport:
Returns whether row `ix` is entirely above the viewport, or `None` before the first layout.

Rows before the scroll position are above the viewport (`Some(true)`) even when they were
never measured. Any other row needs bounds, so it returns `None` if it hasn't been measured.
A zero-height viewport still gives an answer, so the result doesn't flicker while sibling UI
resizes the list.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::item_is_below_viewport:
Returns whether row `ix` is entirely below the viewport, or `None` when the answer isn't known yet.

Rows before the scroll position return `Some(false)`. Other rows follow the rules of
[`Self::item_is_above_viewport`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::logical_scroll_top:
Returns the first visible row, and the pixel offset into that row.

Before the list is scrolled, this is row 0 for [`ListAlignment::Top`]. For
[`ListAlignment::Bottom`] it is the end of the list, the item count, with an offset of zero.
Pass a value you saved to [`Self::scroll_to`] to restore a position.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::max_offset_for_scrollbar:
Returns the largest scroll distance, as a positive `y`.

This is the content height minus the viewport height, using the heights measured so far and
any height hints. During a scrollbar drag it keeps the value from when the drag started.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::measure_all:
Measures every row on the next layout, instead of only the rows that are rendered.

The scrollbar then reflects the full content height from the first frame. The cost is one
render and measure per row, which is slow for a large list. For rows of similar height,
[`Self::with_uniform_item_height`] gives a close estimate without measuring. Measuring runs
again after the width changes, and after [`Self::reset`], [`Self::remeasure`] or
[`Self::remeasure_items`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::new:
Creates the state for a list of `item_count` rows, to store on your view.

`alignment` sets where the list starts: [`ListAlignment::Top`] at the first row, or
[`ListAlignment::Bottom`] at the last row, as a chat log does.

`overdraw` is extra space above and below the viewport. Rows in that space are rendered and
measured, but not painted, so rows that scroll into view are already measured.

Rows start unmeasured. An unmeasured row counts as zero pixels tall until it is rendered,
unless it has a height hint from [`Self::with_uniform_item_height`].

# Examples

```
# use gpui::*;
let state = ListState::new(3, ListAlignment::Top, px(100.));
assert_eq!(state.item_count(), 3);
```
doc_texts.fn:ListState::remeasure:
Marks every row unmeasured, so each is measured again when next rendered.

Use this when all rows change height together, such as when the font size changes. The
scroll position keeps the same fraction of the row at the top of the viewport. For one row
whose content changed, use [`Self::remeasure_items`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::remeasure_items:
Marks the rows in `range` unmeasured, so they are measured again when next rendered.

Use this when a row's content changed height but the row is still at the same index, such as
streaming text. The scroll position is kept. If the row at the top of the viewport is in
`range`, the same pixel offset into that row is kept. Unlike [`Self::splice`], the row count
doesn't change.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::reset_with_uniform_height:
Like [`Self::reset`], and gives every new row the height estimate `height`.

See [`Self::with_uniform_item_height`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::scroll_px_offset_for_scrol:
Returns the current scroll position for the scrollbar, as a negative `y`.

The value is the negation of how far the content has moved, so it is the negative of
[`Self::max_offset_for_scrollbar`] for a bottom-aligned list that is pinned to the end.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::scroll_to_end:
Scrolls past the last row, so the bottom of the list stays in view while the last row grows.

Unlike [`Self::scroll_to_reveal_item`], this anchors to the end of the list, not to a row. The
next paint walks back from the end and shows the bottom of the last row, even while that row
is still growing, as when text streams in. The scroll takes effect on the next paint.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::scrollbar_drag_ended:
Tells the list that the scrollbar drag has ended, so the scrollbar uses the live content
height again. See [`Self::scrollbar_drag_started`].
doc_texts.fn:ListState::scrollbar_drag_started:
Tells the list that the user started dragging its scrollbar.

Until [`Self::scrollbar_drag_ended`], the scrollbar uses the content height from this moment,
so the thumb doesn't move while rows in the overdraw are measured.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::set_offset_from_scrollbar:
Scrolls the list to the position that a scrollbar reports.

`point.y` is a negative scroll offset, as [`Self::scroll_px_offset_for_scrollbar`] returns it.
It is clamped to the content. A drag to the end while the list is in [`FollowMode::Tail`]
resumes following the tail, and any other position stops it. Does nothing before the first paint.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::splice:
Replaces the rows in `old_range` with `count` new, unmeasured rows.

Call this after you add, remove or move rows. Rows after `old_range` keep their measurements
and shift by the change in count. New rows count as zero pixels tall until they are rendered.
If the row at the top of the viewport is in `old_range`, the list scrolls to the start of the
new rows. Use [`Self::splice_focusable`] to keep a focused row rendered.

`splice(old_count..old_count, 1)` appends one row, and `splice(0..0, 1)` inserts one at the top.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::*;
let state = ListState::new(3, ListAlignment::Top, px(0.));
state.splice(1..2, 4); // replace the middle row with four new rows
assert_eq!(state.item_count(), 6);
```
doc_texts.fn:ListState::splice_focusable:
Replaces the rows in `old_range` like [`Self::splice`], and gives each new row an optional focus handle.

Pass `None` for rows that can't take focus. If a row with a focus handle holds focus when it
scrolls out of view, the list keeps rendering it after the visible rows, so keyboard input
still reaches it, until focus moves elsewhere.
doc_texts.fn:ListState::viewport_bounds:
Returns the viewport's bounds in window coordinates, from the last prepaint.

Before the first prepaint this returns empty bounds at the origin.
doc_texts.fn:Menu::disabled: Sets whether the menu is disabled, and returns the menu.
doc_texts.fn:Menu::items:
Replaces the menu's entries with `items`, and returns the menu.

The previous entries are discarded.
doc_texts.fn:Menu::new:
Creates an empty menu with the given title.

Add entries with [`Self::items`].
doc_texts.fn:Menu::owned:
Converts this menu into an [`OwnedMenu`], the form that [`App::get_menus`] returns.

Platforms call this when they store the menu bar set with [`App::set_menus`], so you
rarely need it.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::action:
Returns an entry titled `name` that dispatches `action` when the user picks it.

Use [`Self::os_action`] instead when the entry is a standard command, such as Copy
or Undo.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::checked:
Sets whether the entry shows a checkmark, and returns the entry.

Has an effect only on [`MenuItem::Action`]. Other kinds of entry ignore it.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::disabled:
Sets whether the entry is disabled, and returns the entry.

Has an effect on [`MenuItem::Action`] and [`MenuItem::Submenu`]. Other kinds of entry
ignore it.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::is_checked:
Returns whether the entry shows a checkmark.

Returns `false` for every kind of entry except [`MenuItem::Action`].
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::is_disabled:
Returns whether the entry is disabled.

Returns `false` for separators and system menus.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::os_action:
Returns an entry like [`Self::action`], tagged with the standard command it stands for.

On macOS, Cut, Copy, Paste and Select All are sent to the responder chain, so the
focused text view handles them. Undo, Redo and entries without an `OsAction` dispatch
`action` as usual.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::os_submenu:
Returns a submenu titled `name` that the operating system fills in.

Use it for menus like the macOS Services menu, which the system builds itself.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::owned: Converts this entry into an [`OwnedMenuItem`].
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::separator: Returns a separator entry.
doc_texts.fn:MenuItem::submenu: Returns an entry that opens `menu` as a submenu.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::command:
Returns [`Modifiers`] with only `platform` held: command on macOS, the Windows key on
Windows and the super key on Linux.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::function: Returns [`Modifiers`] with only the function key held.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::modified: Returns whether any modifier key is held.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::number_of_modifiers: Returns how many modifier keys are held.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::secondary_key:
Returns [`Modifiers`] with only the [secondary](Modifiers::secondary) key held: `platform`
on macOS and `control` elsewhere.
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::super_key:
Returns [`Modifiers`] with only the super key held. This is `platform`, the same as
[`Modifiers::command`].
doc_texts.fn:Modifiers::windows:
Returns [`Modifiers`] with only the Windows key held. This is `platform`, the same as
[`Modifiers::command`].
doc_texts.fn:Motion::alternate:
Alternates the direction of successive iterations.

Odd-numbered iterations use the forward pass. Even-numbered iterations use the reverse
pass, or the forward pass when none is configured. This is the same as
`direction(Direction::Alternate)`.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::config: Returns the physical parameters of this spring.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::delay: Returns the delay applied before the first iteration.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::direction: Sets the direction of successive iterations.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::epsilon: Returns the settling tolerance of this spring.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::iterations:
Sets the total number of iterations, including the first.

The default is one. Each iteration restarts local timing. In forward-first alternating
motion, odd-numbered iterations are forward and even-numbered iterations are backward.
With conventional easing endpoints, counts of one and three rest at the target, and counts
of two and four rest at the origin.

# Panics

Panics if `iterations` is zero.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::new: Creates a one-pass linear motion of `duration`, with no delay, run once.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::playback: Returns the iteration count and direction of this motion.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::repeat_forever:
Repeats this motion without end.

Each iteration restarts from the start unless the motion alternates. A motion whose
applicable passes all have zero duration becomes [`MotionPhase::Inactive`], resting at a
deterministic presentation.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::reverse_pass: Returns the reverse pass, or `None` when backward legs reuse the forward pass.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::sample_at:
Samples this motion at `now`, given the time `started_at` when the run began.

`Time` can be any type that subtracts to a [`Duration`](std::time::Duration), such as
[`std::time::Instant`] or the executor's clock.
doc_texts.fn:Motion::spring:
Creates a spring that runs until it settles.

Give the spring a target with [`Motion::to`]. The settling tolerance defaults to `0.001`.
Change it with [`Motion::with_epsilon`].

doc_texts.fn:OngoingScroll::filter:
Zeroes the component of `delta` off the gesture's dominant axis.

The first event of a gesture picks the axis with the larger absolute
movement. Later events keep that axis until the movement clearly favors
the other axis, by at least 1.9 times and at least 6 pixels, and then the
gesture is free on both axes again. A gesture starts again at a
[`TouchPhase::Started`] event, or after 28 milliseconds without an event,
which covers platforms that only send [`TouchPhase::Moved`]. A
[`TouchPhase::Ended`] or [`TouchPhase::Cancelled`] event clears the gesture.

`delta` is in logical pixels and is changed in place. A zero delta on
[`TouchPhase::Started`] clears the gesture, and other zero deltas are
ignored.

# Examples

```
use gpui::{OngoingScroll, Pixels, Point, TouchPhase, point, px};

let mut scroll = OngoingScroll::default();
let mut delta: Point<Pixels> = point(px(10.), px(2.));
scroll.filter(&mut delta, TouchPhase::Started);
// The horizontal movement dominates, so the vertical part is dropped.
assert_eq!(delta, point(px(10.), px(0.)));
```

Gestures are delimited by their touch phase when available, with a timeout
fallback for platforms that only emit [`TouchPhase::Moved`].

doc_texts.fn:ScrollDelta::coalesce:
Merges this delta with a later one, as when two scroll events arrive in
the same frame.

Each axis is handled separately. If both deltas move that axis the same
way, the amounts add. If they move it in opposite directions, `other`
wins on that axis. Two deltas of different kinds, one in pixels and one
in lines, return `other` unchanged.

A component of zero counts as positive, so a zero in `other` replaces a
negative component of `self`, and a zero in `self` is replaced by a
negative component of `other`.

# Examples

```
use gpui::{ScrollDelta, point, px};

// Same direction on x adds (10 + 5); opposite direction on y takes the later 3.
let merged = ScrollDelta::Pixels(point(px(10.), px(-5.)))
    .coalesce(ScrollDelta::Pixels(point(px(5.), px(3.))));
assert_eq!(merged.pixel_delta(px(16.)), point(px(15.), px(3.)));
```
